claims.text: Increasing the cooling rate during processing of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 will enhance its glass-forming ability.
Increasing the cooling rate will improve the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
Standard processing conditions produce a mixture of amorphous and crystalline phases in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Uniform rapid cooling suppresses crystal nucleation.
Geometric or processing constraints that prevent uniform rapid cooling may eliminate the proposed improvement.
Rapid cooling reduces the opportunity for atomic rearrangement leading to crystal nucleation.
Reduced crystal nucleation produces a more stable amorphous structure.
Rapid cooling limits the time available for atoms to organize into a crystalline lattice.
Limiting crystalline organization increases the volume fraction of amorphous material.
Rapid cooling reduces defects and heterogeneities that act as nucleation sites during subsequent thermal treatment.
Reducing defects and heterogeneities thermally stabilizes the amorphous phase.
Higher-rate-cooled samples will have a greater amorphous-phase fraction than conventionally cooled samples.
Higher-rate-cooled samples will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than conventionally cooled samples.
Prior studies establish that the standard cooling rate yields partial amorphization with lower thermal stability.
At sufficiently high cooling rates, thermal gradients and residual stresses may counteract the proposed benefits.
The proposed effect may not persist when composition is changed significantly from Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Earlier literature on similar alloy systems supports the cooling-rate intervention.
The magnitude of improvement may vary with cooling apparatus and sample size.
